newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-SANCHEZ VICARIO CRASHES, SAMPRAS POWERS ON.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SANCHEZ VICARIO CRASHES, SAMPRAS POWERS ON.

text.p: Switzerland's Martina Hingis charged into the last 16 at the Australian Open on Saturday after the abrupt departure of number two seed Arantxa Sanchez Vicario left her facing an almost clear path to the final.
In the men's draw, top seed Pete Sampras looked every inch a champion as he thrashed Australian Mark Woodforde 6-1 6-0 6-1 in their third round tie with a display he felt was virtually flawless.

Hingis, the 16-year-old fourth-seeded prodigy who is seen as the biggest threat to German tennis queen Steffi Graf, hardly put a foot wrong as she disposed of Austria's Barbara Schett 6-2 6-1 in just 50 minutes.
"It was almost a practice, shorter than a practice," an increasingly confident Hingis said after the match.
Hingis and Sampras were the star attractions on a floodlit centre court which had earlier seen Sanchez Vicario turn in her worst grand slam performance for five years.
The Spanish world number three was beaten by little-known Belgian Dominique van Roost 1-6 6-4 8-6 in the biggest upset of the women's draw to date.
Sanchez Vicario, a losing finalist in five of the last eight grand slams, fell away badly after leading 5-2 in the decisive third set to succumb in two hours and 14 minutes.

"She had nothing to lose and everything was on her side. She played very well, but I let go of the match," said Sanchez Vicario, who has won the French and U.S. Opens and was twice a finalist in Melbourne.
Van Roost's reward for beating the gritty Spaniard is a fourth round encounter with American 15th seed Chanda Rubin, who looked in superb touch beating Czech qualifier Sandra Kleinova 6-1 6-3.
Although it was the biggest win of Van Roost's career, the player likely to gain most from Sanchez Vicario's surprise exit was Hingis.

Her next opponent is Ruxandra Dragomir of Romania and the toughest competition she is likely to face on the way to the final is from 15th seed American Chanda Rubin, a semifinalist in Melbourne last year.
In the men's draw, Sampras made it look easy during his victory over veteran doubles specialist Woodforde.

A raucous crowd filled centre court to see the last Australian in the singles draw, hoping to see a repeat of the Saturday night upset last year when big-hitting local star Mark Philippoussis dumped Sampras from the tournament.
But they soon realised that their man had no chance -- a pumped-up Sampras was on near-perfect form but did not intend staying on court any longer than he had to. - in this case 79 minutes.
"I played a great match and everything was really clicking. You just wish you had days like this all the time," said Sampras.
"I don't think I let him get into the match and I played pretty much faultless tennis."
In other matches on Saturday, men's fifth seed Thomas Muster and eighth seed Wayne Ferreira of South Africa cruised through to the last 16, as did Spain's 10th seed Albert Costa.
Big-hitter Goran Ivanisevic hammered his way into the fourth round with a four-set win over American Chris Woodruff which included 26 aces for the Croatian world number three.
Ivanisevic will next play unseeded Norwegian Christian Ruud, who beat South African Neville Godwin.
But 16th seed Alberto Berasategui was forced to retire in the fourth set of his match against Slovakia's Dominik Hrbaty because of leg cramps with Hrbaty leading two sets to one.

Hrbaty, a 19-year-old from Bratislava, made the biggest ranking jump of any player in the top 100, finishing 1996 at 77 from 364. He thrives on slow hard courts, as in Melbourne, dropping only five games in the second round.
But his next opponent, top seed Sampras, said he would not even recognise him if he bumped into him in the locker room.
